abstract.para: The multipathing support in &productname; is based on the Device Mapper Multipath module of the Linux kernel and the multipath-tools user space package.

topic.para: The generic multipathing capability is handled by the Device Mapper Multipath (DM-MP) module.
The packages multipath-tools and kpartx provide tools that handle automatic path discovery and grouping. The tools are the following:

listitem.para: The daemon to set up and monitor multipath maps, and a command-line client to communicate with the daemon process.
The command-line tool for multipath operations.
The command-line tool for managing “partitions” on multipath devices.
The command-line tool for managing SCSI persistent reservations.

section.title: Device mapper multipath module
section.para: The Device Mapper Multipath (DM-MP) module dm-multipath.ko provides the generic multipathing capability for Linux. DM-MPIO is the preferred solution for multipathing on &productname; for SCSI and DASD devices, and can be used for NVMe devices as well.

note.title: Using DM-MP for NVMe devices
note.para: Since &productname; 15, native NVMe multipathing has been recommended for NVMe and used by default. To disable native NVMe multipathing and use device mapper multipath instead (not recommended), boot with the kernel parameter nvme-core.multipath=0.

section.para: The Device Mapper Multipath module handles the following tasks:

listitem.para: Distributing load over multiple paths inside the active path group.
Noticing I/O errors on path devices, and marking these as failed, so that no I/O will be sent to them.
Switching path groups when all paths in the active path group have failed.
Either failing or queuing I/O on the multipath device if all paths have failed, depending on configuration.

section.para: The following tasks are handled by the user-space components in the multipath-tools package, not by the Device Mapper Multipath module:

listitem.para: Discovering devices representing different paths to the same storage device and assembling multipath maps from them.
Collecting path devices with similar properties into path groups.
Monitoring path devices actively for failure or reinstantiation.
Monitoring of addition and removal of path devices.
The Device Mapper Multipath module does not provide an easy-to-use user interface for setup and configuration.

note.title: Failures that multipath prevents
note.para: DM-MPIO protects against failures in the paths to the device, and not failures in the device itself, such as media errors. The latter kind of errors must be prevented by other means, such as replication.

section.title: The multipathd daemon
section.para: multipathd is the most important part of a modern Linux device mapper multipath setup. It is normally started through the systemd service multipathd.service.
multipathd serves the following tasks (some of them depend on the configuration):

listitem.para: On startup, detects path devices and sets up multipath maps from detected devices.
Monitors uevents and device mapper events, adding or removing path mappings to multipath maps as necessary and initiating failover or failback operations.
Sets up new maps on the fly when new path devices are discovered.
Checks path devices at regular intervals to detect failure, and tests failed paths to reinstate them if they become operational again.
When all paths fail, multipathd either fails the map, or switches the map device to queuing mode for a given time interval.
Handles path state changes and switches path groups or regroups paths, as necessary.
Tests paths for “marginal” state, i.e. shaky fabrics conditions that cause path state flipping between operational and non-operational.
Handles SCSI persistent reservation keys for path devices if configured.

note.title: How multipath and multipathd work together
note.para: Many multipathd commands have multipath equivalents. For example, multipathd show topology does the same thing as multipath -ll. The notable difference is that the multipathd command inquires the internal state of the running multipathd daemon, whereas multipath obtains information directly from the kernel and I/O operations.

If the multipath daemon is running, we recommend making modifications to the system by using the multipathd commands. Otherwise, the daemon may notice configuration changes and react to them. In some situations, the daemon might even try to undo the applied changes. multipath automatically delegates certain possibly dangerous commands, like destroying and flushing maps, to multipathd if a running daemon is detected.

section.para: The list below describes frequently used multipathd commands:

listitem.para: Shows the current map topology and properties.
Shows the currently known path devices.
Shows the currently known path devices using a format string. Use show wildcards to see a list of supported format specifiers.
Shows the currently configured map devices.
Shows the currently configured map devices using a format string. Use show wildcards to see a list of supported format specifiers.
Shows the current configuration that multipathd is using.

Rereads configuration files, rescans devices, and sets up maps again. This is basically equivalent to a restart of multipathd. A few options cannot be modified without a restart. They are mentioned in the man page multipath.conf(5). The reconfigure command reloads only map devices that have changed in some way. To force the reloading of every map device, use reconfigure all (available since &sles; 15 SP4; on previous versions, reconfigure reloaded every map).
Unconfigure and delete the given map device and its partitions. MAP DEVICE NAME can be a device node name like dm-0, a WWID, or a map name. The command fails if the device is in use.

varlistentry.term: switchgroup map MAP DEVICE NAME group N

listitem.para: Switch to the path group with the given numeric index (starting at 1). This is useful for maps with manual failback.

section.para: Additional commands are available to modify path states, enable or disable queuing, and more. See multipathd(8) for details.

section.title: The multipath command
section.para: Even though multipath setup is mostly automatic and handled by multipathd, multipath is still useful for some administration tasks. Several examples of the command usage follow:

listitem.para: Detects path devices and configures all multipath maps that it finds.
Similar to multipath, but does not set up any maps (“dry run”).

Configures a specific multipath device. DEVICENAME can denote a member path device by its device node name (/dev/sdb) or device number in major:minor format. Alternatively, it can be the WWID or name of a multipath map.
Unconfigures ("flushes") a multipath map and its partition mappings. The command will fail if the map or one of its partitions is in use. See above for possible values of DEVICENAME.
Unconfigures ("flushes") all multipath maps and their partition mappings. The command will fail for maps in use.
Displays the status and topology of all currently configured multipath devices.
Displays the status of a specified multipath device. See above for possible values of DEVICENAME.
Shows the internal hardware table and the active configuration of multipath. Refer to multipath.conf(5) for details about the configuration parameters.
Has a similar function to the multipath -t command but shows only hardware entries matching the hardware detected on the host.

section.para: The option -v controls the verbosity of the output. The provided value overrides the verbosity option in /etc/multipath.conf.

section.title: SCSI persistent reservations and mpathpersist
section.para: The mpathpersist utility is used to manage SCSI persistent reservations on Device Mapper Multipath devices. Persistent reservations serve to restrict access to SCSI Logical Units to certain SCSI initiators. In multipath configurations, it is important to use the same reservation keys for all I_T nexuses (paths) for a given volume; otherwise, creating a reservation on one path device would cause I/O errors on other paths.

Use this utility with the reservation_key attribute in the /etc/multipath.conf file to set persistent reservations for SCSI devices. If (and only if) this option is set, the multipathd daemon checks persistent reservations for newly discovered paths or reinstated paths.
You can add the attribute to the defaults section or the multipaths section of multipath.conf. For example:
After setting the reservation_key parameter for all mpath devices applicable for persistent management, reload the configuration using multipathd reconfigure.

note.title: Using “reservation_key file”
note.para: If the special value reservation_key file is used in the defaults section of multipath.conf, reservation keys can be managed dynamically in the file /etc/multipath/prkeys using mpathpersist.
This is the recommended way to handle persistent reservations with multipath maps. It is available from &productname; 12 SP4.

section.para: Use the command mpathpersist to query and set persistent reservations for multipath maps consisting of SCSI devices. Refer to the manual page mpathpersist(8) for details. The command-line options are the same as those of the sg_persist from the sg3_utils package. The sg_persist(8) manual page explains the semantics of the options in detail.

In the following examples, DEVICE denotes a device mapper multipath device like /dev/mapper/mpatha. The commands below are listed with long options for better readability. All options have single-letter replacements, like in mpathpersist -oGS 123abc DEVICE.

listitem.para: Read the registered reservation keys for the device.
Show existing reservations for the device.
Register a reservation key for the device. This will add the reservation key for all I_T nexuses (path devices) on the host.
Create a reservation of type 5 (“write exclusive - registrants only”) for the device, using the previously registered key.
Release a reservation of type 5 for the device.
Delete a previously existing reservation key from the device.
